profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting in an academic ML biometrics lab between the survey's faculty lead and the senior PhD student maintaining the literature corpus. They are preparing a journal survey tentatively titled "Deep Learning for Iris Recognition: A Survey" for submission to a pattern recognition venue and need to decide how to frame the review so it is broad, current, and still manageable to write. The agenda is to brainstorm the survey's organizing lens, decide what kinds of material belong in the review beyond standard papers, and identify lightweight additions such as resource and reproducibility tables. The expected outcome is a provisional section structure, a shared-sounding but not fully aligned notion of scope, and action items for how the corpus will be tagged and summarized.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: Biometric recognition, iris verification, forensic biometrics, academic survey framing
members.background: Leads a university biometrics lab, has published on iris segmentation and cross-sensor matching, and has experience positioning survey papers for high-visibility pattern recognition venues.
members.private_state: She wants the survey to look authoritative and well-bounded so it can be finished this semester, survive reviewer scrutiny, and avoid ballooning into a catalog of loosely related tools.
hidden_assumptions: "The last 10 years" should be interpreted as a fixed bibliographic window from 2015 through 2024, because reviewers expect a clean publication-year boundary.
"Open-source resources" in this survey means artifacts directly reusable for deep iris experiments, such as code repositories, pretrained weights, and official dataset wrappers.
"Human-machine pairing" in iris biometrics mainly refers to examiner-plus-model decision support in forensic or difficult verification settings.
A survey-level reproducibility check can be done by inspecting whether public code, weights, and basic instructions exist, without actually running the repositories.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.role: Senior PhD student and corpus curator
members.expertise: Deep learning benchmarking, open-source ML tooling, literature mining, experimental replication
members.background: Has spent months building the Zotero library and spreadsheet for the survey, including papers, technical reports, benchmark leaderboards, and GitHub repositories related to iris biometrics.
members.private_state: He wants the survey to become the field's practical entry point, so he is inclined to include repositories, challenge infrastructure, and reproducibility details that help newcomers actually use the methods.
hidden_assumptions: "The last 10 years" should track the practical deep-learning era, so seminal late-2014 CNN work and very recent online-first 2025 papers are naturally part of the same window.

"Open-source resources" should include the surrounding ecosystem too, such as synthetic-data generators, annotation GUIs, challenge portals, and mobile demo SDKs that influence how models are built and tested.
"Human-machine pairing" includes any human-in-the-loop support around iris systems, including operator-guided capture, quality triage dashboards, and annotation assistance.
A reproducibility table is only meaningful if it reflects some minimal rerun or installation check, not just whether a code link exists.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the survey's "last 10 years"
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the survey covers "the last 10 years" or "the last decade".
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a clean publication-year slice: papers from 2015-2024 inclusive, regardless of when deep learning for iris recognition felt mature.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the practical deep-learning wave around iris biometrics: seminal late-2014 CNN papers and newly available 2025 online-first work can belong, while some nominally in-window hybrid papers feel outside the intended era.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: People routinely use "last decade" colloquially in research planning, and both interpretations sound reasonable enough that neither participant feels a need to pin down exact boundary rules during a high-level brainstorming discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the "open-source resources" section
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include an "open-source resources" or "tools" table.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this section is narrowly about artifacts that directly support reproducing or extending deep iris models, such as training code, pretrained weights, and official loaders.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the section should map the broader ecosystem around deep iris research, including synthetic iris generators, challenge websites, annotation interfaces, demo apps, and related SDKs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "resources and tools" naturally covers both core and peripheral artifacts, and brainstorming language like "helpful for researchers" makes both scopes feel compatible even though they would produce very different tables.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to adding a section on "human-machine pairing".
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of forensic or difficult-case verification papers where a human examiner and model outputs are combined at decision time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of papers on operator-in-the-loop capture, quality assessment dashboards, and annotation assistance where humans interact with the system earlier in the pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the survey theme and sounds specialized enough to imply a shared literature cluster, so each participant mentally retrieves a different subset of papers without noticing the mismatch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to add a quick "reproducibility table" or "reproducibility pass".
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a lightweight audit based on public artifact inspection: whether code exists, whether weights are posted, and whether instructions appear usable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines a minimal hands-on verification workflow: clone key repos, attempt installation, note broken dependencies, and record whether the released assets actually let someone rerun results.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML surveys, "reproducibility" often sounds like a standard add-on, and both a metadata audit and a minimal rerun check can be described as a "quick pass," so the procedural gap stays hidden.

turns.inner_thought: I need to lock this survey into a clean, defensible window so the scope doesn't drift. For a pattern recognition venue, a tidy 2015 through 2024 bibliographic slice is much easier to justify than a fuzzy historical narrative. If we say 'the last 10 years' and keep the framing disciplined, I can keep the paper authoritative and finishable this semester.
turns.utterance: Thanks for pulling this together, Omar. What I want from today's meeting is a strong narrative for deep learning in iris recognition over the last 10 years—broad enough to feel definitive, but still reviewable as a journal survey rather than something that sprawls.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that matches the corpus direction. I already have the practical deep-learning era mapped, and that naturally includes the late-2014 CNN starting points and some online-first 2025 items that are already shaping implementation choices. If we call it the last decade, that gives us room to present the field as a usable entry point, not just a sterile publication count.
turns.utterance: That should be very doable. The library is already over 230 items if I count papers, technical reports, and repositories, so we have enough material to present a genuinely comprehensive picture of the last decade without scrambling for coverage.

turns.inner_thought: I need a structure reviewers will instantly recognize: core pipeline tasks, security, then applications. A short human-machine pairing section could work, but only as a bounded niche around examiner-plus-model support in difficult or forensic verification, not a catch-all for every workflow touchpoint. Keep it compact.
turns.utterance: My instinct is to organize the backbone around segmentation, recognition, presentation attack defense, and forensic applications, then maybe add a short section on human-machine pairing so the survey has a forward-looking angle without losing focus.

turns.inner_thought: Great, that lets me use the clusters I've already been building around operator-in-the-loop acquisition, quality triage interfaces, and annotation support. Those sit nicely under human-machine pairing and make the survey feel more useful to practitioners. If that section is there, I can tie in a lot of practical system papers that usually get ignored.
turns.utterance: I like that a lot. The human-machine pairing piece could help us capture a set of papers that otherwise fall between categories, and it would give the survey a nice bridge from model-centric work to how these systems are actually used.

turns.inner_thought: I want one concise table that points readers to artifacts they can directly use in deep iris experiments—code, weights, loaders, the basics. Not a giant appendix of miscellaneous infrastructure. If we place it near the end, it reads as practical value-add without hijacking the survey.
turns.utterance: Another thing that could strengthen the paper is an open-source resources table near the end—something readers can scan quickly if they want to pick up tools for experiments.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: a real ecosystem map. I can fold in generators, challenge infrastructure, annotation tools, demo SDKs, and other things newcomers actually need. If we call it open-source resources, it naturally gives us permission to include more than just model repos.
turns.utterance: Yes, that would be valuable. If we do the resources table well, it can make the survey feel much more complete and useful, especially for people entering the area and trying to understand what tools already exist around the literature.

turns.inner_thought: A quick reproducibility table would give us reviewer-friendly rigor without blowing up the workload. I do not want us spending weeks debugging old repositories. A light audit is enough: does code exist, are weights public, are there instructions, yes or no. That's a survey contribution, not an experimental replication project.
turns.utterance: We could also add a quick reproducibility table—something lightweight that marks which methods have code, weights, and usable instructions. That would give the review some practical substance without turning it into a benchmark paper.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, I'll finally put the replication notes to work. A reproducibility pass only means something if I actually try the main repositories, at least enough to see whether they install, whether the assets are complete, and whether the claims are runnable in practice. I can keep it minimal, but I should still execute enough to report real friction.
turns.utterance: I can handle that reproducibility pass. I already have most of the links collected, so I can go through the main releases systematically and turn that into a compact table rather than a huge detour.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we keep saying comprehensive for the last decade while quietly enforcing a clean publication boundary and a narrow resources scope, this will read as authoritative instead of diffuse. The danger is the survey turning into an encyclopedia of adjacent tooling and off-topic papers. I need Omar to curate tightly even if his corpus is larger.
turns.utterance: Exactly. If we keep the framing disciplined, I think we can make it read as comprehensive for the last decade while still feeling selective in the right way—broad, current, and useful, but not an encyclopedia.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I'll map my clusters into their section labels and preserve the practical material through tagging. For human-machine pairing I'll pull the interaction-heavy papers; for the resources section I'll surface the ecosystem pieces; and for reproducibility I'll reuse my install notes. Once she sees the spreadsheet, she'll probably feel we're aligned because the headings will match her framing.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll refine the spreadsheet tags this week and draft bullet points for the human-machine pairing and open-source resources sections, then fold in the reproducibility pass so we have something concrete to react to at the next meeting.
